content: Biguanides, classified under ATC A10BA, represent a group of oral antihyperglycemic medications primarily used for the treatment of diabetes mellitus and prediabetes. Examples of Biguanides: Metformin: This is the most widely used biguanide for managing type 2 diabetes, particularly in patients who are also obese. Phenformin: This drug has been withdrawn from the market in most countries due to its association with toxic effects, particularly lactic acidosis. Buformin: Similar to phenformin, this drug was also removed from the market because of its toxic effects. Proguanil: Unlike the other biguanides, proguanil is not used for diabetes treatment but instead serves as an antimalarial agent. History: The plant Galega officinalis was traditionally used for centuries in the treatment of diabetes. In the 1920s, guanidine compounds were identified in extracts of Galega. Animal studies demonstrated that these compounds could lower blood glucose levels. Less toxic derivatives, such as Syntalin A and Syntalin B, were briefly used for diabetes management. However, after the discovery of insulin, these compounds fell out of favor for several decades. Biguanides were reintroduced for the treatment of type 2 diabetes in the late 1950s. Among them, metformin emerged as the safest and most effective option, becoming the primary biguanide used in pharmacotherapy worldwide. Pharmacotherapy: Biguanides differ from other hypoglycemic agents, such as sulfonylureas and meglitinides, in that they do not stimulate insulin secretion. As a result, they are effective not only in type 2 diabetes but can also be used in type 1 diabetes when combined with insulin therapy. Mode of Action: The precise mechanism of action of biguanides is not fully understood. However, in cases of hyperinsulinemia, biguanides can reduce fasting plasma insulin levels. Their therapeutic effects are largely attributed to their ability to suppress hepatic gluconeogenesis, thereby lowering blood glucose levels. Additionally, biguanides enhance the sensitivity of peripheral tissues to insulin, promoting glucose uptake by cells and further reducing plasma glucose concentrations. Side Effects and Toxicity: The most common side effects of biguanides include gastrointestinal disturbances such as diarrhea and dyspepsia, which occur in up to 30% of patients. The most serious adverse effect is lactic acidosis, a rare but potentially fatal condition. Phenformin and buformin are more likely to cause lactic acidosis compared to metformin, which is why they have been largely replaced by metformin in clinical practice. However, when metformin is used in combination with other drugs (combination therapy), there is a risk of hypoglycemia and other side effects.
